title: "...have real-world relevance without importing the outside world directly into every course."
author: Lance Eaton (interviewer); Priten Shah
summary: This is the second part of a published interview between Lance Eaton and Priten Shah, author of Ethical Ed Tech: How Educators Can Lead on AI & Digital Safety in K-12, continuing their exploration of AI, education systems, and the gap between research and practice. Shah argues that systemic problems—inadequate educator compensation, misaligned incentive structures, and the difficulty of the universal-education project in an unequal society—prevent education research from reaching classrooms, and that AI adoption has so far accelerated institutional purchasing rather than actual educator literacy. He distinguishes sharply between a can/will gap (students can use AI productively but mostly won't because incentives reward shortcuts), and a can/should gap (the more important moral question). Shah warns that speeding up classroom AI integration without first speeding up educator tech literacy creates a dangerous mismatch, and cautions against treating AI as a magic bullet for pre-existing systemic failures. He also argues that students graduating into AI-saturated job markets do not necessarily need to have used AI in college—what matters is foundational critical thinking and adaptability, not familiarity with specific tools.
points: The gap between educational research and classroom practice is structural, not just attitudinal: inadequate teacher compensation, adjunct-heavy higher-ed labor, and systems that reward research over teaching all prevent implementation.

Shah's 'can vs. will' distinction matters: AI can enable students to improve their writing or thinking, but the incentive structures of higher education actively reward shortcuts, so most students will use AI for performance rather than learning.

Institutions are signing massive AI contracts and running company-led PD, but actual educator usage remains low months later—indicating adoption is being accelerated without literacy being built at matching speed.
Shah argues there is 'a major mismatch' in urgency: we are not building broad educator AI literacy as quickly as we are signing institutional deals with AI companies.

On the job market question, Shah challenges the hype: no current AI leader learned about AI in a formal college course, and foundational intellectual skills—reading, writing, critical thinking—remain the more important preparation for any student.
quotes: There is a gap between can and will. I talk a lot about can versus should, because that's the important moral question we need to deliberate on. But there is also a gap between can and will.

Students already wanted shortcuts. We were clearly not getting through to them, and the technology has simply given them one more easy path. I don't think it has created some massive new crisis that didn't exist before. We were walking past that crisis and pretending it didn't exist.
We are not building broad literacy among educators as quickly as we are building institutional buy-in for purchasing tools. There is a major mismatch there.

A district or institution signs for a tool, brings in company-led professional development, and then three months later maybe four teachers are actively using it. That suggests we are accelerating adoption without accelerating literacy.
When I say slow down, I mean slow down the assumption that these tools are going to be magic bullets for all of our problems. That's the part we need to slow down on.
